text: The Ottoman Empire, ruled from Istanbul, was losing wars because its armies could not keep up with Europe’s.
Sultan Mahmud II began to change the way the empire was run, in the style of the West.
src: The Ottoman Empire: Istanbul and the provinces / led to defeats in the Russo-Turkish Wars and the Greek War of Independence (1821–1830), and exposed the empire’s inability to compete with European armies
from then on his reign was one of Western reform and centralization, on which the Tanzimat built

text: In 1839 the Tanzimat began, an age of reform, or changes meant to make things better.
A royal order promised every subject safety of life, property and honour, and fair taxes.
src: The Tanzimat was the age of Ottoman reform from the Edict of Gülhane of 1839
The Edict of Gülhane promised every subject security of life, property and honour, fair taxation and conscription, and public trials

text: The order was named after the rose house in the grounds of the Topkapı Palace.
Later, a new order promised that people of all religions would be equal before the law.
src: named after the rose house in the grounds of the Topkapı Palace
The Imperial Reform Edict of 1856 promised full legal equality for citizens of all religions

text: The empire built new schools and universities, railways, telegraph lines and banks.
The slave market of Istanbul was closed in 1847.
src: new ministries, schools and universities, secular courts and codes, the Mecelle, railways, telegraphs and banks
The Istanbul Slave Market was closed in 1847

text: Statesmen, more than the sultans, led the changes.
In 1876 Midhat Pasha wrote a constitution, a set of rules for how the country was to be run.
src: The Tanzimat was driven by reforming statesmen rather than by the sultans
Midhat Pasha led the ministers who deposed Abdul Aziz and wrote the constitution of 1876

text: But borrowing money left the empire bankrupt, unable to pay its debts, in 1875, and Balkan peoples rose up.
Historians still argue whether the reforms made the state stronger or helped it break apart.
src: Foreign loans brought bankruptcy in 1875 / Balkan risings
historians still dispute whether they strengthened the state or hastened its break-up
